title: Straight, round, back and forth: the paths moving things take

summary.text: Make a bunch of keys go round and round on a string. Look down from above, and you see a circle. Put your eyes at the same height, and the same keys seem to go back and forth, like a swing. Things move in three main paths: straight, round, and back and forth. Your child finds all three at home, sorts things that move by themselves from things that are moved, and tests whether they can walk straight with their eyes shut.
summary.art: A girl lying on a tiled floor with her chin on her hands, watching a bunch of keys go round on a string held by an adult, with a dotted circle drawn round the keys from above and a straight dotted line drawn from the girl's side view.

intro.hook: Draw a straight line in the air with your finger. Now draw a circle. Now wave your finger back and forth. Those are the three paths.
intro.text: A path is the way a thing goes as it moves. A ball rolled down a corridor goes in a straight line. The tip of a fan blade goes round and round. A swing goes back and forth. Some things start moving by themselves, like an ant or a crow. Others move only when something pushes or pulls them, like a ball. In this unit you hunt for all three paths, and test one surprise: can a round path look like a back-and-forth one?
intro.art: A girl in a flat drawing three paths in the air with her finger: a straight arrow, a circle and a line with arrows at both ends, while a crow sits on the window grille.

outcomes: By the end I can name the three paths things move in: straight, round, and back and forth.
By the end I can find things at home that move in each path, and things that move in two paths at once.
By the end I can show that a round motion, seen from the side, looks like back and forth.
By the end I can sort things into those that move by themselves and those that are moved by a push or pull.
By the end I can say why I need my eyes to keep walking in a straight line.
By the end I can make a guess, test it, count what I see, and say what I found.

terms.meaning: A path is the way a thing goes as it moves. You can draw it as a line.
terms.example: The path of a ball rolled along the corridor is a straight line.
terms.art: A ball on a tiled floor with a dotted line behind it showing where it has rolled.

terms.meaning: Straight motion is moving along a straight line, without turning.
terms.example: A drawer sliding open, a lift going up, and a train on a straight track all move straight.
terms.art: A long straight railway track with a train on it and a straight arrow above.

terms.meaning: Round motion is going round and round a middle point, along a circle. Scientists call it circular motion.
terms.example: The tip of a fan blade and a seat on a giant wheel both go round.
terms.art: A giant wheel at a mela with a curved arrow going round it.

terms.meaning: Back-and-forth motion is going one way, then back the other way, again and again.
terms.example: A swing, a cradle and a toothbrush scrubbing your teeth all move back and forth.
terms.art: A cloth cradle hanging from a ceiling hook, with a curved arrow pointing both ways under it.

terms.meaning: To vibrate is to move back and forth very fast, often too fast to see. Vibrating things often make a sound.
terms.example: A ruler flicked on the edge of a table vibrates and buzzes.
terms.art: A ruler held on the edge of a table, its free end drawn blurry with little sound lines.

terms.meaning: A living being moves by themselves when they start, stop and turn with no push or pull from outside. They use energy from their food.
terms.example: An ant walking to a sugar grain and a crow flying off the grille both move by themselves.
terms.art: An ant walking along a kitchen counter towards a grain of sugar.

terms.meaning: A thing is moved when a push or a pull from something else starts it or keeps it going. A push or a pull is called a force.
terms.example: A ball moves when your foot kicks it. A curtain moves when the wind blows it.
terms.art: A child's foot kicking a ball, and a curtain blowing in from an open window.

explanations.definition: Most moving things move in one of three paths: straight, round, or back and forth.
explanations.description: In straight motion, a thing goes along a line and does not turn. In round motion, it goes round a middle point, along a circle. In back-and-forth motion, it goes one way and then back again, over and over. Back-and-forth motion that is very small and fast is called vibrating.
examples: A drawer slides straight out and straight back in.
A clock's hands go round the middle of the clock.
A cradle rocks back and forth.
explanations.context: This card is about the three paths you hunted for at home: straight, round, and back and forth.
explanations.art: Three small drawings in a row: a drawer with a straight arrow, a clock face with a curved arrow round it, and a cradle with an arrow pointing both ways.

explanations.concept: One thing, two paths at once
explanations.definition: Different parts of one thing can move in different paths at the same time.
explanations.description: When a cycle rides along a straight road, the whole cycle moves straight. At the same time, its wheels and pedals go round. The rider's knees go up and down, back and forth. So when we ask how something moves, we need to ask which part we are watching.
examples: An auto goes straight along the road while its wheels go round.
A sewing machine's wheel goes round while its needle goes up and down.
When you walk straight down the corridor, your arms swing back and forth.
explanations.context: This card is about things that move in two paths at once, like a cycle.
explanations.art: A girl riding a cycle along a straight road, with a straight arrow above the cycle and curved arrows round the wheels and pedals.

explanations.concept: Round motion seen from the side
explanations.definition: A thing going round in a circle looks like it goes back and forth when you watch from the side, at the same height.
explanations.description: From above, you saw the keys go round in a circle. From the side, you could not see them coming towards you or going away. You saw only their left and right, so they seemed to go back and forth, like a swing. Their shadow on the wall did the same.
examples: In the keys test, 10 rounds from above matched about 10 back-and-forths from the side.
A fan's blade tips go round. A gecko on the wall, level with the fan, would see them go back and forth.
Galileo saw Jupiter's moons go back and forth beside Jupiter. They are going round Jupiter, and we see their circles from the side.
explanations.context: This card is about the keys test, where you watched keys going round on a string from above and from the side.
explanations.art: Two pictures side by side: keys going round on a string seen from above as a circle, and the same keys seen from the side as a straight line with arrows at both ends.

explanations.concept: Moving by themselves, or being moved
explanations.definition: Living beings start, stop and turn by themselves. Most things that are not alive start moving only when a push or a pull starts them.
explanations.description: An ant decides where to walk, and a crow decides when to fly. They use energy from their food to move their own bodies. A ball, a door and a curtain start moving only when something pushes or pulls them: a foot, a hand or the wind. A fan, a lift or an auto has a motor or engine, so electricity or fuel starts it, not a push. People still argue about what 'by themselves' really means.
examples: A pigeon walks along the window ledge by herself.
A leaf moves when the wind blows it.
A ceiling fan goes round when electricity turns its motor, and slows down and stops when the power goes.

perspectives.who: Aristotle, a Greek thinker who lived about 2,400 years ago
perspectives.explanation: Everything that moves is moved by something. In an animal, one part of her body moves another part.
Every mover needs a push from something. An ant moves forward by pushing the floor back with her feet. A fish pushes the water. So nothing starts moving with no push at all.
What is special about living beings is that they choose when and where to move, and use their food's energy to do it.

explanations.context: This card is about the Who Starts It? watch, where you sorted moving things by what started them.
explanations.art: A window with a crow flying off the grille, a curtain blowing in the wind, and a ceiling fan turning inside the room.

agreed.text: Things move in straight, round and back-and-forth paths, and one thing can move in more than one path at once.
agreed.evidence: A cycle goes straight along the road while its wheels and pedals go round. A sewing machine's wheel goes round while its needle goes up and down.

agreed.text: A round motion watched from the side looks like back and forth.
agreed.evidence: Keys going round on a string look like a swing from the side, and so does their shadow on a wall. Jupiter's moons, which go round Jupiter, look from Earth as if they go back and forth beside it.

agreed.text: Living beings use energy from their food to move themselves.
agreed.evidence: Muscles need food to work. After running and playing for a long time, you feel tired and hungry.

challenging.claim: A round path and a back-and-forth path are always easy to tell apart.
challenging.for: From above, a circle and a swing look very different.
challenging.against: In the shadow game, the shadow of keys going round looked almost the same as the shadow of keys swinging. Galileo first took Jupiter's moons for ordinary stars in a line, until he saw them change places from night to night.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that round and back-and-forth paths always look different.

challenging.claim: Only living beings move by themselves.
challenging.for: Ants, crows and people start and stop when they choose. A ball lies still until someone kicks it.
challenging.against: A fan, a lift and an auto start without anyone pushing them, using electricity or fuel. So a push is not the only thing that starts a motion.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that only living beings move by themselves.

challenging.claim: Plants stay still. They do not move by themselves.
challenging.who: A common idea, because plants move too slowly for us to notice
challenging.for: A potted plant seems to stay in the same place all day.
challenging.against: Seedlings by a window lean towards the light in a day or two, and lean back if you turn the pot. Touch-me-not plants fold up their leaves within seconds of a touch.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that plants never move.

big_questions.q: The keys went round the whole time. Why did they seem to go back and forth from the side?
big_questions.hint: From the side, could you tell when the keys were coming towards you or going away?

big_questions.q: Why did your walk drift off the line when your eyes were shut?
big_questions.hint: With your eyes open, what tells you that you have started to turn?

big_questions.q: The Earth goes round the Sun. Seen from very far away, from the side, what path would the Earth seem to take?
big_questions.hint: Think of the keys seen from the side, and of Jupiter's moons.

big_questions.q: When you decide to get up and walk, where does the start of that walk come from?
big_questions.hint: Think about what you ate, and what you wanted to do.

story.title: Revathi and the Shadow on the Wall
text: Revathi was seven. She lived on the fourth floor of a block of flats in Hyderabad, with her Amma and her Ammamma. Ammamma is her grandmother. That week her cousin Arjun was staying with them. He was six.
One evening, the lights went out. The ceiling fan kept turning, slower and slower, and then it stopped.
"Power cut," said Amma. She put her phone on the dining table, with its torch shining at the white wall.
Ammamma's bunch of keys hung on a long red thread from her waist. Revathi untied them. "Can I play with these, Ammamma?"
"Gently," said Ammamma. "And keep them away from faces."
Revathi stood near the wall and held the thread. She moved her hand in a tiny circle. The keys went round and round below it. Their big black shadow moved on the wall.
Arjun was on the sofa. "You're swinging them," he said. "Like an uyyala."
"I'm not swinging," said Revathi. "They're going round. Look down at them."
"I can only see the shadow," said Arjun. "And it's going back and forth."
Revathi frowned. She gave Arjun the keys. "You do it. Make a tiny circle with your hand. Slowly." She showed him how. Then she sat on the sofa, where Arjun had been.
She looked at the wall. The shadow went to the left, then to the right, then to the left again. It looked exactly like a swing.
"Are you swinging them?" she asked.
"No! You told me to go round," said Arjun.
Revathi got up and looked down at the keys from above. They were going round in a circle. She sat down on the sofa again. Back and forth. She got up again. Round.
"It's the same keys," she said slowly. "From the top, they go round. From the side, they go back and forth."
"So which is it?" asked Arjun.
"Let's test," said Revathi. "I'll shut my eyes. You make them swing, or go round. Then I'll open my eyes and look only at the shadow. I'll guess which."
She guessed five times. She was right twice and wrong three times. "I can't tell from the shadow!" she said. "I have to look from the top."

Ammamma laughed. "A long time ago, a scientist called Galileo looked at Jupiter through a telescope. He saw little moons going back and forth beside Jupiter. He worked out that they were really going round it. We see their circles from the side."
Just then a moth flew in from the balcony. She flew round and round the torch. On the wall, an ant was walking in a straight line towards the kitchen.
"Who is pushing the ant?" asked Arjun.
"Nobody," said Revathi. "She moves by herself. She decides where to go."
"And the keys?" asked Ammamma.
"The keys go only where my hand moves them," said Revathi. "And the moth moves by herself, like the ant."
With a click, the power came back. The fan began to turn again.
"The fan moved by itself!" said Arjun.
"No," said Revathi. "The electricity came back. It turns the motor inside the fan. When the power went, the fan slowed down and stopped."
That night, Revathi lay in bed and looked up at the fan. From below, the blades went round in a circle. On the wall near the ceiling sat a little house gecko.
"Ammamma," Revathi whispered. "The gecko is level with the fan. I think the gecko sees the blades go back and forth."
"You may be right," said Ammamma. "Go to sleep now."
story.note: Hyderabad is a real city in Telangana. Ammamma means mother's mother in Telugu. An uyyala is a swing seat that hangs in many homes in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh. Revathi, Arjun, Amma and Ammamma are made up. Galileo Galilei was a real scientist who saw Jupiter's moons in 1610.
story.epiphany: For the parent: Arjun sees the shadow go back and forth, and Revathi sees the keys go round. Both are right about what they see. Revathi tests it by guessing from the shadow alone, and finds she cannot tell. One motion looks round from above and back and forth from the side. Then the ant, the moth, the keys and the fan show the difference between moving by yourself, being moved, and having a motor.
ask: Why did Arjun think Revathi was swinging the keys?
How did Revathi test whether she could tell round from back and forth?
Who moved by themselves in the story, and what was moved?
Why did the fan start again?
art: A dim room in a flat during a power cut, a phone torch on the dining table shining on a white wall, and a girl holding a bunch of keys on a red thread so their shadow falls on the wall.
A boy on a sofa pointing at a shadow of keys on the wall, while the girl looks down at the keys going round below her hand.
A moth flying round a phone torch, and a small ant walking in a straight line along the wall.
A girl lying in bed looking up at a turning ceiling fan, with a little gecko on the wall near the ceiling.

experiments.title: Round or Back and Forth? Keys on a string, seen from two places
experiments.context: This is the main experiment of the unit. You make a bunch of keys go round and round on a string. Then you watch them from above, from the side, and as a shadow on the wall.
experiments.question: Keys go round and round in a circle on a string. What path do you see when you watch from the side, with your eyes at the same height as the keys?
experiments.predict: Guess first. From the side, will you see a circle, a straight line, or something else? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same string, the same keys and the same slow speed every time. Only the place we watch from changes. We count 10 rounds each time, so we can compare the counts.

materials.item: a string or thick thread about as long as your arm
a bunch of keys, or a lemon tied in a hanky, to hang on the string
a phone torch or a torch
a plain wall in a room you can make dim
paper and a pencil for the table

experiments.safety: Keep the keys going slowly, and keep everyone's face at least one big step away from them.

schedule.what: Make the keys go round, guess, watch from above and from the side, count, and play the shadow game.

experiments.record: Draw the keys seen from above, with their path. Then draw them seen from the side, with their path. Write the two counts.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results
rows: Back and forth, like a swing

setup.art: An adult standing on a tiled floor, holding a string with a bunch of keys hanging near the floor, the hand making a tiny circle, and the keys going round in a big circle drawn with a dotted line.
setup.caption: 1. Hold the string. Make a tiny circle with your hand. The keys go round.

setup.art: A girl standing beside the adult, looking straight down at the keys, with a circle drawn round them.
setup.caption: 2. Look down from above. What path do you see?

setup.art: The same girl lying on her tummy two steps away, her chin on her hands and her eyes level with the keys, and a straight line with arrows at both ends drawn through the keys.
setup.caption: 3. Get your eyes down low. Look from the side.

setup.art: A dim room with a phone torch on a table shining at a wall, the keys going round between them, and the shadow on the wall drawn with arrows at both ends.
setup.caption: 4. Watch the shadow on the wall. Round or swinging?

flow.do: 1. Tie the keys to one end of the string. 2. Hold the other end so the keys hang just below your knee. 3. Move your hand in a tiny, slow circle until the keys go round in a circle about the size of a plate.
flow.say: Watch. I move my hand in a tiny circle. The keys go round in a big circle under my hand.
flow.kid: Watch the keys. They go round and round under the hand.
flow.parent: Small, steady hand circles make a neat circle. If the keys start to swing back and forth instead, stop them and start again with a smaller circle.

flow.do: 1. Keep the keys going round. 2. Ask for a guess and a reason. 3. Write the guess down.
flow.say: If you get down low and look from the side, what will you see? A circle, a line, or something else? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess. From the side, what path will the keys make? Why?

good: A circle, because they go round.
A line, because I will only see one side.
I don't know. I will have to look.

flow.parent: Write the guess in your child's own words. Do not explain yet.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands next to you and looks straight down at the keys. 2. Keep the keys going round. 3. Count 10 rounds together, out loud.
flow.say: Look straight down from the top. What path do the keys make? Count each time they come back to your side.
flow.kid: Look down at the keys. What shape do they make? Count 10 rounds.

ask.q: What path did you see from the top?
good: A circle.
Round and round.

flow.do: 1. Your child lies on the floor 2 big steps away, with chin on hands and eyes as low as the keys (or sits on the floor). 2. Keep the keys going round exactly as before. 3. Your child says 'tick' each time the keys reach the left end. 4. You count 10 rounds.
flow.say: Now put your eyes as low as the keys. Say tick each time they reach the left end. What path do you see now?
flow.kid: Lie down. Look from the side. Say tick at the left end.

ask.q: What path did you see from the side?
good: They go side to side.
Back and forth, like a swing.
A straight line.

flow.parent: From the side, the keys seem to go only left and right, like a swing. While you count 10 rounds, your child should count about 10 ticks. One round looks like one back and forth.

flow.do: 1. Make the room dim. 2. Put the phone torch on a table, shining at a plain wall. 3. Hold the keys between the torch and the wall, close to the wall and as high as the torch. 4. Your child looks only at the shadow. 5. Make the keys go round, then swing them back and forth, in any order.
flow.say: Look only at the shadow on the wall. Am I making the keys go round, or swing back and forth? Tell me which.
flow.kid: Look only at the shadow. Are the keys going round or swinging? Can you tell?
flow.parent: The shadow of keys going round and the shadow of keys swinging look almost the same. A sharp-eyed child may notice that a swing's shadow rises a little at each end. That is a good find. Let your child try the shadow game on you too.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the table together. 2. Ask what your child saw, and why it looked different.
flow.say: From the top you saw a circle. From the side you saw back and forth. Were the keys doing two things, or one thing?
flow.kid: From the top, a circle. From the side, back and forth. Did the keys change?

ask.q: Why did the keys look different?
good: They went round all the time. I looked from a different place.
From the side I could not see them come closer and go away.

flow.parent: Now explain. From the side, you cannot see the keys coming towards you and going away. You only see them go left and right. So a round motion seen from the side looks like a back-and-forth motion.

check.q: The keys went round in a circle on the string. What did you see from the side, with your eyes low?
options: Back and forth, like a swing
check.why: From the side you see only the keys' left and right, so a round path looks like back and forth.

flow.think: Where else might something going round look like it goes back and forth?

experiments.title: Eyes Shut, Walk Straight: can you stay on the line?
experiments.context: In this experiment you walk along a straight line, first with your eyes open and then with your eyes shut. You find out how far you drift from the line.
experiments.question: Can you walk 8 steps along a straight line with your eyes shut, and stay on it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. With your eyes shut, will you stay on the line, or drift off it? If you drift, which way? Why do you think so?
experiments.fair_test: We use the same line, the same start and the same 8 steps every time. Only the eyes change: open or shut. We try eyes open 2 times and eyes shut 3 times, because one try can be a fluke.
results_table: How many hand-widths from the line I stopped

materials.item: a straight line on the floor about 8 small steps long: the line between two rows of tiles, or a strip of tape
a clear floor with no toys or furniture in the way
a paper slip to mark where you stop

experiments.safety: Clear the floor first. A grown-up walks beside the child all the time and stops them before any wall, door or corner.

schedule.what: Guess, walk the line twice with eyes open and three times with eyes shut, mark each stop, and measure in hand-widths.

experiments.record: Draw the line. Draw a dot for each place you stopped: blue for eyes open, red for eyes shut.

setup.art: A tiled floor with a long straight line between two rows of tiles, and a girl standing with her toes on one end of it.
setup.caption: 1. Stand with your toes on the line.

setup.art: The girl walking along the line with her eyes shut, an adult walking close beside her with one hand ready.
setup.caption: 2. Shut your eyes. Walk 8 steps. A grown-up walks beside you.

setup.art: The girl stopped, a paper slip by her toes, and her hand laid flat on the floor between her toes and the line to measure.
setup.caption: 3. Stop. Measure the gap to the line in hand-widths.

flow.do: 1. Find a straight tile line, or stick down a strip of tape. 2. Clear the floor around it. 3. Show your child where to start.
flow.say: This is our straight line. You will stand at this end and walk 8 steps along it.
flow.kid: This is the line. Stand at this end with your toes on it.
flow.parent: A tile line in a hall or corridor works well. You need about 8 small steps of clear floor, plus a little more at the end.

flow.do: Ask for a guess and a reason, and write it down.
flow.say: First with eyes open, then with eyes shut. Will you stay on the line with your eyes shut? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: With your eyes shut, will you stay on the line? Why?

good: Yes, because I know where the line is.
No, because I can't see it.
I might go a bit to one side.

flow.do: 1. Your child walks 8 steps along the line with eyes open. 2. Put a slip at their toes. 3. Measure the gap to the line in hand-widths of your child's hand. 4. Do it twice.
flow.say: Walk 8 steps along the line with your eyes open. Stop. How far are your toes from the line?
flow.kid: Eyes open. Walk 8 steps on the line. Stop. Look at your toes.
flow.parent: With eyes open, most children stay on the line or very close to it.

flow.do: 1. Your child stands at the start and shuts their eyes. 2. Walk close beside them while they take 8 steps. 3. Put a slip at their toes. 4. Measure the gap in hand-widths. 5. Do it 3 times.
flow.say: Now shut your eyes. Walk 8 steps, as straight as you can. I am right beside you. Stop. Now open your eyes.
flow.kid: Shut your eyes. Walk 8 steps. A grown-up is beside you. Stop and look.

ask.q: What did you see when you opened your eyes?
good: I was off the line.
I went to one side.
I was nearly on it.

flow.parent: Most people drift off the line with their eyes shut, often by a hand-width or more in 8 steps. Some walk almost straight one time and drift the next. Both are real results.

flow.do: 1. Fill in the table together. 2. Compare eyes open with eyes shut. 3. Ask why.
flow.say: Which tries stayed closest to the line? Why do you think your eyes help you walk straight?
flow.kid: Look at the table. When did you stay closest? Why?

good: I can see the line.
I can see when I start to turn, and fix it.

flow.parent: Now explain. With eyes open, you see every tiny turn and fix it straight away. With eyes shut, tiny turns add up and nothing tells you to fix them. Scientists tested people walking with their eyes covered in a big field, and many walked in circles.

check.q: Why did you drift off the line with your eyes shut?
options: I could not see my small turns to fix them
check.why: Your eyes show you each small turn so you can fix it. With your eyes shut, the small turns add up.

flow.think: How do you think a person who is blind walks straight along a road?

activities.title: Path Hunt: straight, round, or back and forth?
activities.context: In this activity you hunt round your home for things that move. For each one, you draw its path in the air with your finger and add a tick to the right column.

materials.item: a sheet of paper with three columns: STRAIGHT, ROUND, BACK AND FORTH
a pencil

activities.safety: Watch the ceiling fan and the mixie from a distance. Never touch moving blades.

schedule.what: Find moving things, draw each path in the air, and tick the columns.

activities.record: Tick one column for each thing you find. Draw one thing from each column.

setup.art: A sheet of paper with three columns headed STRAIGHT, ROUND and BACK AND FORTH, with a straight arrow, a circle and a two-headed arrow at the top.
setup.caption: 1. Make a sheet with three columns.

setup.art: A girl opening a drawer and drawing a straight line in the air with her other hand.
setup.caption: 2. Make a thing move. Draw its path in the air.

setup.art: The same girl ticking the STRAIGHT column on the sheet.
setup.caption: 3. Put a tick in the right column.

flow.do: 1. Draw three columns on paper. 2. Draw a straight arrow, a circle and a two-headed arrow at the top. 3. Read the words together.
flow.say: Here are the three paths: straight, round, and back and forth. Draw each one in the air with your finger.
flow.kid: Draw each path in the air. Straight. Round. Back and forth.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home together. 2. For each moving thing, your child draws its path in the air. 3. They tick the right column.
flow.say: Open the drawer. What path did it take? Draw it in the air. Now which column gets a tick?
flow.kid: Make it move. Draw its path in the air. Tick a column.

ask.q: What path does a door take when it opens?
good: Part of a circle.
It goes round its hinges.
Round, but only a little bit.

flow.parent: Good finds: a drawer and water from a tap go straight. A clock's hands and a fan go round. A toothbrush, a curtain in the breeze and a cradle go back and forth. A door turns round its hinges, so the edge of a door makes part of a circle.

flow.do: 1. Count the ticks in each column. 2. Ask which column has the most.
flow.say: Which column has the most ticks? Did anything fit two columns?
flow.kid: Count the ticks. Which column has the most?

check.q: Water falls from a tap into a bucket. What path does the water take?
check.why: Water falls down along a straight line, so it moves straight.

activities.title: Who Starts It? Watch from the window and sort
activities.context: In this activity you watch from a window and around your home. For each moving thing, you ask: did it start by itself, did a push or pull start it, or does it have a motor?

materials.item: a window that looks out on a road, a tree or other buildings
a sheet of paper with three columns: BY THEMSELVES, PUSHED OR PULLED, MOTOR OR ENGINE
a pencil

schedule.what: Watch for 5 minutes, sort each moving thing, then add things inside the home.

activities.record: Draw one thing in each column.

setup.art: A girl and an adult at a window with a grille, looking out at a crow on a wire, clothes moving on a line and an auto on the road.
setup.caption: 1. Watch from the window for 5 minutes.

setup.art: A sheet with three columns headed BY THEMSELVES, PUSHED OR PULLED and MOTOR OR ENGINE, with small drawings of a crow, a waving cloth and an auto.
setup.caption: 2. Sort each moving thing into a column.

flow.do: 1. Draw the three columns on paper. 2. Explain each one with an example.
flow.say: Some things start moving by themselves, like you. Some need a push or a pull. Some have a motor or an engine inside.
flow.kid: Three columns. By themselves. Pushed or pulled. Motor or engine.

flow.do: 1. Watch from the window together for 5 minutes. 2. For each moving thing, ask what started it. 3. Your child draws or writes it in a column.
flow.say: Look, a crow flew off the wire. Did anything push the crow? Which column is that?
flow.kid: Find a moving thing. What started it? Put it in a column.

ask.q: What started the clothes on the line moving?
good: The wind pushed them.
The air moved them.

flow.parent: Crows, pigeons, people and dogs move by themselves. Leaves, clothes on a line and a kite are moved by the wind. Autos, buses, scooters and lifts have engines or motors.

flow.do: 1. Add things from inside the home: the fan, a ball, an ant, the door, you. 2. Talk about any that are hard to sort.
flow.say: Now the fan. Does it move by itself, or is it moved? What happens to the fan in a power cut?
flow.kid: Now look inside. The fan. A ball. An ant. You. Which column?

ask.q: Which one was hardest to sort? Why?
good: The fan, because nobody pushes it but it needs electricity.
A plant, because plants move very slowly.

flow.parent: There is no single right answer for a fan. It has a motor, so nobody pushes it, but it stops when the power goes. Praise a good reason.

check.q: Which of these has a motor or an engine that starts it moving?
check.why: An auto has an engine, so fuel starts it, not a push. A leaf is moved by the wind, and a crow moves by herself.

activities.title: Buzz the Ruler: back and forth too fast to see
activities.context: In this activity you flick a ruler on the edge of a table. It goes back and forth so fast that it blurs and buzzes. This fast back-and-forth motion is called vibrating.

materials.item: a ruler or steel scale, about 30 cm long
a table with a hard edge

schedule.what: Flick the ruler with a long end and a short end sticking out, and feel your throat while you hum.

activities.record: Draw the ruler on the table, with arrows at both ends of its free end.

setup.art: A ruler lying on a table with half of it sticking out over the edge, and a girl's hand pressing the part on the table down firmly.
setup.caption: 1. Press one end of the ruler on the table.

setup.art: The girl's other finger flicking the free end down, the end drawn blurry with arrows up and down.
setup.caption: 2. Flick the free end. Watch and listen.

flow.do: 1. Lay the ruler on the table with about half sticking out. 2. Your child presses the table end down hard. 3. They flick the free end down.
flow.say: Press this end down hard. Now flick the other end. What does it do?
flow.kid: Press one end down. Flick the other end. Watch it move.

ask.q: What path does the end of the ruler take?
good: Up and down, back and forth.
It goes up and down very fast.

flow.do: 1. Slide the ruler so only a short part sticks out. 2. Flick again. 3. Compare the long end and the short end.
flow.say: Now only a little part sticks out. Flick it. Is it faster or slower? Is the buzz higher or lower?
flow.kid: Make the end short. Flick it. Faster or slower?
flow.parent: A long free end moves back and forth slowly enough to see. A short end moves so fast it blurs, and the buzz sounds higher.

flow.do: 1. Your child puts two fingers gently on the front of their throat. 2. They hum.
flow.say: Put your fingers on your throat and hum. What do you feel?
flow.kid: Fingers on your throat. Hum. Can you feel a buzz?
flow.parent: Your child feels a tingle. Parts inside the throat vibrate back and forth very fast when we hum or talk.

check.q: A ruler moves back and forth very fast and buzzes. What is that called?
check.why: Moving back and forth very fast is called vibrating.

games.title: Three Paths: the card game
games.players: A child and a grown-up. More children can join and take turns.
games.context: This is a card game. The grown-up reads what each card shows. The player draws its path in the air, then puts the card on the STRAIGHT, ROUND or BACK AND FORTH mat.

items.f: A Mumbai local train on a straight track
A seat on a giant wheel at a mela

img.credit: Ростислав Александрович Луценко, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.f: A cradle rocking in the hall
A lift going up
The tip of a ceiling fan blade
A toothbrush scrubbing teeth
A drawer sliding open
The hands of a clock
An oar rowing a boat across a river
A coconut falling from a tree

img.credit: Raja Sekhar Chimirala, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: A cycle on a straight road
items.b: STRAIGHT for the cycle, ROUND for the wheels

items.f: A sewing machine needle
items.b: BACK AND FORTH, up and down

rules: Cut out the three mats and lay them on the floor.
The grown-up reads the front of one card out loud.
The player draws the path in the air with a finger, then puts the card on a mat.
The grown-up reads the back. If the player is right, the player keeps the card. If the back names two paths, the player must say which part moves in each path.
If the player gives a good reason for a different mat, the player keeps the card too.
A card that is wrong goes back to the bottom of the pile. After 12 cards have been tried, count the cards each player kept. The most cards wins. If you play alone, try to keep more than 8.

setup.art: Three sheets of paper on the floor labelled STRAIGHT, ROUND and BACK AND FORTH, with an arrow, a circle and a two-headed arrow.
setup.caption: 1. Lay out the three mats.

setup.art: A girl drawing a circle in the air with her finger while holding a card, and an adult holding the other cards.
setup.caption: 2. Draw the path in the air. Put the card on a mat.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the three mats and lay them on the floor. 2. Draw each path in the air together.
flow.say: Here are three mats. Draw a straight line in the air. Now a circle. Now back and forth.
flow.kid: Draw each path in the air. Straight. Round. Back and forth.

flow.do: 1. Read the cards one by one. 2. Your child draws the path in the air and puts the card on a mat.
flow.say: A seat on a giant wheel. Draw its path in the air. Which mat does it go on?
flow.kid: Listen. Draw the path in the air. Put the card on a mat.

ask.q: Why does the cycle card fit two mats?
good: The cycle goes straight, but the wheels go round.
Different parts move in different paths.

flow.parent: Some cards fit two mats. Praise a reason that says which part moves which way. Children take turns with the cards.

flow.do: Count the cards each player kept.
flow.say: Who kept the most cards? Did any card fit two mats?
flow.kid: Count the cards you kept.

check.q: An oar pushes a boat through the water, again and again. What path does the oar take?
check.why: The oar goes one way through the water, then comes back for the next stroke, so it moves back and forth.

games.title: Who Starts It? The quick-hands card game
games.players: 2 or more players. A grown-up can play too.
games.context: This is a quick game. One player reads a card and the other players show with their hands what starts that thing moving: itself, a push or pull, or a motor.

items.f: An ant walking to a grain of sugar

img.credit: Joss Carr, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: A football after a kick
A ceiling fan
A crow flying off the window grille
A kite in the sky at Sankranti
items.b: PUSHED by the wind, and PULLED by the string

items.f: An auto on the road
You, walking to the kitchen
A door closing in the wind
A lift going up
A fish swimming in a pond

img.credit: Utain Pummarin, CC BY, via iNaturalist

items.f: A pulled cart of vegetables
Mustard seedlings leaning to the window

rules: Agree on three hand signs: hands on your chest for BY THEMSELVES, pushing palms for PUSHED OR PULLED, and rolling fists for MOTOR.
Shuffle the cards and deal them out equally. Each player has a pile. With 2 players, you have 6 cards each.
Take turns. The reader reads the front of one card and does not show a sign.
Everyone else shows a sign as fast as they can.
The reader reads the back. Everyone with the right sign gets a point.
A player who gives a good reason for a different sign also gets a point.
Play until all 12 cards are read. The most points wins. If it is a tie, everyone wins.

setup.art: Three children showing three hand signs: hands on chest, palms pushing forward, and fists rolling round each other.
setup.caption: 1. Learn the three hand signs.

setup.art: An adult reading a card while two children show their signs.
setup.caption: 2. Listen to the card. Show a sign fast.

flow.do: Teach the three hand signs and practise each one.
flow.say: Hands on your chest means the thing moves by itself. Pushing palms means a push or pull. Rolling fists means a motor.
flow.kid: Learn the signs. Chest, pushing palms, rolling fists.

flow.do: 1. Deal the cards. 2. The reader reads a card and the others show a sign. 3. Read the back and give points. 4. Next player reads.
flow.say: A kite in the sky at Sankranti. What starts it moving? Show your sign!
flow.kid: Listen. What starts it moving? Show your sign fast!

ask.q: Why did you show pushing palms for the kite?
good: The wind pushes it.
The string pulls it.

flow.parent: The seedlings card surprises many children. Plants move by themselves, but slowly, over hours and days.

flow.do: Count the points.
flow.say: Who has the most points? Which card made you think the hardest?
flow.kid: Count your points. Which card was hardest?

check.q: A fish swims to the top of the pond for food. What starts the fish moving?
check.why: A fish moves on her own, using her fins and tail and the energy from her food.

projects.title: The Seedlings Who Lean to the Light
projects.context: In this project you grow mustard or methi seedlings in a cup. Then you put them by a window and watch them move by themselves, very slowly, towards the light.

materials.item: a pinch of mustard seeds (rai or kadugu) or methi seeds
a small steel cup or a paper cup
cotton wool or a folded tissue
water
a window that gets daylight

schedule.what: Put wet cotton in the cup and sprinkle the seeds on top. Keep it in the middle of a room, away from the window.
Check the seeds. Add a few drops of water if the cotton feels dry.
Look for tiny shoots. When most are about 2 cm tall, put the cup on the window sill.
Look at the seedlings from the side. Which way do they lean? Draw them. Then turn the cup halfway round.
Look again. Which way do they lean now? Draw them.
Talk about what happened. Did the seedlings move by themselves?

projects.record: Draw the seedlings on day 4 and day 5, with an arrow pointing to the window.

setup.art: A small steel cup with wet cotton inside and tiny round mustard seeds sprinkled on top.
setup.caption: 1. Sprinkle seeds on wet cotton in a cup.

setup.art: The cup on a window sill, with tiny green seedlings all leaning towards the window glass.
setup.caption: 2. Put the cup by the window. Watch which way they lean.

setup.art: The same cup turned halfway round, and the next day the seedlings leaning back towards the window.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cup round. Look again the next day.

flow.do: 1. Put wet cotton in the cup. 2. Your child sprinkles a pinch of seeds on top. 3. Keep it in the middle of a room.
flow.say: These seeds will grow into tiny plants. Sprinkle them on the wet cotton. We keep the cup away from the window for now.
flow.kid: Sprinkle the seeds on the wet cotton. Keep the cotton wet.
flow.parent: Mustard seeds usually sprout in 1 to 2 days in a warm room. Methi takes 2 to 3 days. In a cold room, wait a day or two longer.
flow.wait: Check every day until shoots are about 2 cm tall

flow.do: 1. When the shoots are about 2 cm tall, put the cup on the window sill. 2. The next day, look from the side together. 3. Your child draws them.
flow.say: Look at the seedlings from the side. Are they standing straight? Which way are they leaning?
flow.kid: Look from the side. Which way do the seedlings lean?

good: Towards the window.
To the light.

flow.wait: Leave the cup on the window sill for 1 day

flow.do: 1. Turn the cup halfway round, so the seedlings now lean away from the window. 2. Ask for a guess.
flow.say: Now they lean away from the window. What will they do by tomorrow? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Turn the cup round. What will the seedlings do by tomorrow?
flow.wait: Leave the cup for 1 more day

flow.do: 1. Look from the side again. 2. Compare with yesterday's drawing.
flow.say: Which way do they lean now? Who moved them?
flow.kid: Look again. Which way do they lean now?

ask.q: Did the seedlings move by themselves?
good: Yes, they turned back to the light.
Yes, but very slowly.

flow.parent: The seedlings sense where the light comes from. The shaded side of each stem grows faster than the lit side, so the stem bends towards the light. They move by themselves, just too slowly to watch.

check.q: You turn the cup so the seedlings lean away from the window. What happens the next day?
options: They lean back towards the window
check.why: Seedlings bend towards the light by themselves, so they turn back towards the window.

challenges.title: Draw a Round Path Without Tracing
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. Can you draw a good circle without tracing round a bangle, a plate or anything else?
challenges.problem: You want to draw a big circle for a kolam, but you have no plate big enough to trace round. Can you draw a round path, as big as your hand-span or bigger, without tracing anything?
constraints: You may not trace round anything.
The circle must be at least as wide as your hand-span.
materials: a pencil or a sketch pen
a ruler or a strip of card
general: A compass in a geometry box holds one point still while the pencil goes round it.
A string held still at one end and tied to a pencil at the other end keeps the pencil the same distance from the middle.
Kolam artists in Tamil Nadu draw smooth curves freehand with rice flour after a lot of practice.
creative: Hold the string still with one finger in the middle, and pull the pencil round on the tight string.
Keep the pencil still and turn the paper round under it, like a potter's wheel.
Use your own arm: keep your elbow still on the paper and swing your hand round.
Poke a pencil through a hole at one end of a strip of card, and pin the other end down with a finger.
challenges.your_turn: Try two ways to draw a circle. Which circle came out rounder? Why do you think so?

setup.art: A sheet of newspaper with a dot in the middle, a string held on the dot by a finger, and a pencil tied to the other end drawing a circle.
setup.caption: 1. Hold one end still. Move the pencil round.

setup.art: A pencil held still on paper while a girl turns the paper round underneath it, a circle appearing.
setup.caption: 2. Or keep the pencil still and turn the paper.

flow.do: Read the problem together and ask for ideas.
flow.say: We need a big circle and have no plate to trace. How could you keep the pencil going round one middle point?
flow.kid: How can you draw a circle with nothing to trace round?

good: A middle point.
Every bit the same distance from the middle.

flow.do: 1. Your child tries one idea. 2. Then a second idea.
flow.say: Try your first idea. Now try another one. Which circle is rounder?
flow.kid: Try one way. Now try another way. Which is rounder?
flow.parent: Holding the middle of a string still is the hardest part. A grown-up can hold the middle while the child pulls the pencil round.

flow.do: Compare the circles and ask why one worked better.
flow.say: Which circle came out rounder? What kept the pencil going round the same middle?
flow.kid: Which circle is rounder? Why?

check.q: You tie a pencil to a string and hold the other end still. Why does the pencil go round in a circle?
options: The string keeps it the same distance from the middle
check.why: A tight string keeps the pencil the same distance from the still middle, and that makes a circle.

items.p: Draw a line from each thing to its path.
pairs: A seat on a giant wheel
items.why: A fan blade and a giant wheel seat go round a middle point. A lift and a drawer move along a straight line. A swing goes one way and back again.

items.p: Draw the keys on a string as you saw them from above. Then draw them as you saw them from the side. Draw the path each time.
items.a: From above: keys with a circle round them. From the side: keys with a straight line and arrows at both ends.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a circle from above and a back-and-forth line from the side.
items.art: Two blank boxes, one labelled FROM ABOVE and one labelled FROM THE SIDE.

items.p: Circle in green the things that move by themselves. Circle in blue the things that are moved by a push or pull.
items.why: Ants, crows and people start moving by themselves. A ball, a door and a leaf move when a foot or the wind pushes them.

items.p: A cycle can go straight along the road while its wheels go round.
items.why: True. The whole cycle moves straight, and at the same time each wheel goes round its middle.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why did the shadow on the wall look like a swing, when the keys were going round?
items.a: Because the shadow showed only the left and right of the keys, not their coming closer and going away.
items.why: A strong answer says the keys were really going round, and that from the side we see only their left and right.

items.p: Three of these move in a straight line. Which one does not?
opts: A train on a straight track
items.why: A clock's hands go round the middle of the clock. The others move along a straight line.

items.p: Look at the girl on the cycle. Under each part, say STRAIGHT or ROUND, and a grown-up writes it.
labels: The whole cycle on the road
items.why: The wheels and pedals go round their middles while the whole cycle goes straight along the road.
items.art: A girl riding a cycle along a straight road, with arrows pointing to the wheels, the pedals and the whole cycle.

items.p: A swing goes back and ___.
items.why: A swing goes one way, then back the other way, again and again: back and forth.

items.p: A clock's minute hand goes round once in one hour. How many times does it go round in 3 hours?
items.why: One hour is one round. So 3 hours are 3 rounds.

items.p: Mustard seedlings by a window lean towards the light by themselves, very slowly.
items.why: True. The seedlings sense the light and bend towards it. They move by themselves, too slowly to watch.

items.p: Kavya and her friend Farhan look at the ceiling fan.

views.says: The fan moves by itself. Nobody pushes it.
The fan is moved. Electricity turns its motor. In a power cut, it stops.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Say why. Then say one thing the other person might say back.
items.a: Both have a point. Nobody pushes the fan, so it seems to move by itself. But it needs electricity to turn its motor, and it slows and stops in a power cut.
items.why: A strong answer uses what happens in a power cut. It also sees why the other person thinks so.

items.p: Draw the path of the tip of a fan blade, as you see it lying under the fan. Then draw what a gecko on the wall, level with the fan, would see.
items.a: From below: a circle. From the wall: a straight line with arrows at both ends.
items.why: A strong drawing shows a circle from below and back and forth from the side, like the keys test.
items.art: Two blank boxes, one labelled FROM BELOW and one labelled FROM THE WALL.

items.p: Say out loud, and a grown-up writes it down: why do you need your eyes to walk in a straight line?
items.a: My eyes show me when I start to turn, so I can fix it. With my eyes shut, the small turns add up.
items.why: A strong answer uses the eyes-shut test and says that eyes help us notice and fix small turns.

items.p: Put the seedling project in order.
items: See them lean back to the window
Sow the seeds on wet cotton
Put the cup by the window and see them lean
a: Sow the seeds on wet cotton
Put the cup by the window and see them lean
See them lean back to the window
items.why: First the seeds grow, then they lean to the light, then we turn the cup, and then they lean back.

items.p: Only things that are alive can move.
items.why: False. A ball, a leaf and a door move too, when something pushes or pulls them. Living beings are the ones that start moving by themselves.

items.p: Under each picture, say STRAIGHT, ROUND or BACK AND FORTH, and a grown-up writes it.
labels: A Mumbai local train on a straight track
items.why: The train goes along a line, the merry-go-round goes round its middle, and the cradle and the oar go one way and back again.
items.art: Four small pictures: a local train, a merry-go-round, a cloth cradle and a boat with an oar.

items.p: Sort these into STRAIGHT, ROUND and BACK AND FORTH.
items: A coconut falling from a tree
The Moon going round the Earth
A ruler buzzing on a table
items.why: Falling and lifts go along a line. The Moon and a potter's wheel go round a middle. A buzzing ruler and a toothbrush go one way and back.

items.p: Name one thing that moves in two paths at the same time. Say which part moves which way.
items.a: For example, a cycle: it goes straight and its wheels go round. Or a sewing machine: the wheel goes round and the needle goes up and down.
items.why: A strong answer names two parts of one thing and gives each part its own path.

items.p: Mira, a girl in Class 2, puts her fingers on the front of her throat and hums. What does she feel?
opts: Nothing, because the throat stays still
A buzz, because parts inside her throat vibrate
items.why: Parts inside the throat move back and forth very fast when we hum. Moving back and forth very fast is called vibrating.

items.p: A clock's second hand goes round once in one minute. How many times does it go round in 5 minutes?
items.why: One minute is one round. So 5 minutes are 5 rounds.

items.p: Meenakshi, Anu and their friend Ravi see a shadow on the wall going back and forth.

views.says: The thing making the shadow is swinging.
It might be going round. From the side, round looks like back and forth.
We cannot know until we look at the thing itself from above.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Say why, using the keys test. Then say what Meenakshi might say back.
items.a: Anu and Ravi. In the keys test, the shadow of keys going round looked like a swing. Looking from above shows which it is.
items.why: A strong answer uses the shadow game as evidence and sees that Meenakshi could still be right: a swing also makes that shadow.

items.p: Galileo saw Jupiter's moons go back and forth beside Jupiter, night after night. Why did he decide they were going round Jupiter?
items.a: Because something going round, seen from the side, looks like it goes back and forth, and the moons never went far from Jupiter.
items.why: A strong answer links Jupiter's moons to the keys seen from the side.

items.p: Nisha, a girl in Class 2, says a ball lying still will start rolling by itself if you wait long enough. Draw how you would test this. What do you expect to see?
items.a: A ball on a flat floor and a clock. The ball stays still until something pushes it or the floor slopes.
items.why: A strong plan uses a flat floor, waits a set time, and changes nothing else. It expects the ball to stay still unless a push or a slope starts it.

items.p: A ceiling fan keeps going round for a little while after the power goes off.
items.why: True. The fan keeps turning for a few seconds after the motor stops, and slows down until it stops.

items.p: Asha, a girl in Class 2, says, 'Plants cannot move by themselves.' How would you test what Asha says?
items.a: Grow seedlings by a window, see them lean to the light, turn the cup, and see them lean back by the next day.
items.why: A strong answer describes a test, like the seedling project, where the plant moves with nobody touching the plant.

items.p: Match each mover to what starts it moving.
pairs: A rowing boat on a river
items.why: The ant and the crow move themselves. The fan has a motor. The kite and the boat are moved by the wind, a string and people.

items.p: A wheel rolls along a straight road. What path does the middle of the wheel take?
items.why: The rim goes round the middle, but the middle itself goes straight along the road with the cycle.

items.p: Sort these into BY THEMSELVES, PUSHED OR PULLED, and MOTOR.
items: Clothes on a line in the wind
A cart pulled by a man
items.why: Pigeons and goats move themselves. A lift and a mixie have motors. Clothes and a cart are moved by the wind and by a person.

items.p: Kalpana, a girl in Class 2, watches a giant wheel go round 3 times. She stands to the side of the wheel. Her friend's seat goes up and down. How many times does the seat reach the top?
items.why: Each time the wheel goes round once, the seat goes up to the top once. So 3 rounds make 3 trips to the top.

items.p: Three of these are moved by a push or a pull. Which one is not?
opts: A curtain blowing in the wind
A cart pulled by a man
items.why: A lift has a motor that starts it. The football, the curtain and the cart are moved by a foot, the wind and a person.

quiz.p: Which of these moves in a straight line?
quiz.why: A lift moves along a straight line. A fan goes round, and a swing goes back and forth.
A potter's wheel turns round its middle.

quiz.p: A cradle rocks in the hall. What path does it take?
quiz.why: A cradle goes one way, then back again, over and over.

quiz.p: A girl walks straight down the corridor. What path do her arms take?
quiz.why: While she walks straight, her arms swing back and forth. One body can move in two paths at once.

quiz.p: An auto goes along a straight road. What do its wheels do?
quiz.why: The auto goes straight while each wheel goes round its middle.

quiz.p: A gecko sits on the wall, level with a ceiling fan. The fan blades go round. What path do the blades seem to take to the gecko?
opts: The blades seem to stand still
quiz.why: From the side, the gecko sees only the left and right of each blade, so a round path looks like back and forth.

quiz.p: Which of these moves by themselves?
quiz.why: A crow starts and stops by herself. A football and a curtain need a push from a foot or the wind.

quiz.p: Which of these is moved by the wind?
quiz.why: The wind pushes the kite. The ant and the goat move themselves.

quiz.p: You walk 8 steps on a line with your eyes shut. What usually happens?
opts: You stay exactly on the line
You drift off the line a little
quiz.why: Without your eyes, small turns add up and you drift.

quiz.p: Gopal, a boy in Class 2, guesses the keys will look round from every side. What should he do next?
opts: Test it by looking from the side
Ask a friend and believe them
quiz.why: A guess is checked by a test. Gopal can lie down and look from the side.

videos.title: Jupiter and its moons, a six hour time-lapse
videos.why: Shows the moons going back and forth beside Jupiter, as Galileo saw them, because we see their circles from the side.
videos.check: Found by search: "Jupiter and Its Moons - Six Hour Timelapse" by Ted Judah, 27 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: Tomato seedlings bending towards light, a time-lapse
videos.why: Shows seedlings moving by themselves towards a light, as in the seedling project.
videos.check: Found by search: "Phototropism Time Lapse | Tomato Seedlings Reaching for the Sun" by MOTH, 18 seconds. A parent may preview it.

videos.title: A ball going round in a circle and its shadow moving back and forth
videos.why: Shows a round motion and its back-and-forth shadow side by side, as in the keys test. Short, with no talking needed.
videos.check: Found by search: "1D10.50 Simple Harmonic Motion and Uniform Circular Motion" by Brown Physics Demos, 26 seconds. A parent may preview it.

applications: Trains, lifts and drawers run on straight tracks or rails so they move in a straight line.
Wheels, fans, mixie blades and washing machine drums go round to do their work.
Old clocks used a swinging pendulum, a weight going back and forth, to keep time.
Sewing machines turn round motion into the needle's up-and-down motion.
Cradles and swings rock babies and children back and forth.
Engineers use circles to work out how swings and springs move back and forth.

spotted.text: Boatmen pulling their oars back and forth at the ghats in Varanasi.

open_questions.q: Why do people walk in circles when they cannot see?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists tested people walking with their eyes covered in a big field, and many walked in circles. Each person drifted in their own way. Scientists are still working out exactly why the small turns build up.

open_questions.q: How does a seedling sense which way the light is coming from?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have found light-sensing parts in plant cells, and a growth chemical that gathers on the shaded side of the stem. How a seedling puts all these signals together to choose the best way to bend is still being studied.

maths.problem: In the story, Revathi counted 12 rounds of her keys from above. Her cousin Arjun watched from the side and counted the back-and-forths. Arjun counted 12 too. Why did the counts match?
maths.answer: Because one round looks like one back and forth from the side. So 12 rounds look like 12 back-and-forths.
maths.explain: Each time the keys go round once, they reach the left end once. So the number of ticks from the side is the same as the number of rounds from above. Matching counts show it was one motion seen two ways.
maths.context: This is about the keys test, where you watched keys going round from above and from the side.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the two counts shows that the round path and the back-and-forth path were the same motion.

maths.problem: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 2, did the eyes-shut test. She stopped 0 and 0 hand-widths from the line with her eyes open. With her eyes shut she stopped 1, 3 and 2 hand-widths away. Which try was furthest from the line? What do the numbers tell you about eyes?
maths.answer: The second eyes-shut try, at 3 hand-widths. Every eyes-shut try was further from the line than every eyes-open try.
maths.explain: 3 is the biggest number, so that try drifted most. All the eyes-shut numbers are bigger than 0. So eyes help Lakshmi stay on the line, even though each eyes-shut try was different.
maths.context: This is about the eyes-shut test, where you walked 8 steps along a line.
maths.why_maths: Comparing the numbers shows a pattern: eyes shut always meant further from the line.

maths.problem: Fatima, a girl in Class 2, did the Path Hunt. She ticked 5 things for STRAIGHT, 4 for ROUND and 3 for BACK AND FORTH. Draw a tally for each. How many things did she find in all? Which path did she find most?
maths.answer: 12 things in all. STRAIGHT had the most, with 5.
maths.explain: 5 and 4 make 9, and 3 more makes 12. 5 is the biggest number, so straight things were the most common in her home.
maths.context: This is about the Path Hunt, where you ticked three columns for moving things at home.
maths.why_maths: Tallies make it easy to see which kind of path is most common in a home, and to ask why.

roots.context: We have found straight, round and back-and-forth paths, and watched keys on a string from two places. Now we ask what the keys test tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: From above, the keys on your string went round in a circle. From the side, they went back and forth, once for every round. The keys kept the same path all the time. So round and back-and-forth can be one motion, seen from two places.
deep_truth.habit: We sort motions into kinds, such as round and back and forth, as if each kind were a separate thing. The keys test showed that one motion fits two kinds, depending on where it is watched from.
deep_truth.evidence: In the keys test, 10 rounds seen from above matched about 10 back-and-forths seen from the side, and the shadow on the wall went back and forth too.

three.who_am_i: You move yourself. You decide to walk, turn and stop, and your eyes keep you on your path.
three.what_is_life: Living beings start, stop and turn by themselves. An ant, a crow and a mustard seedling each move towards what they need.
three.what_is_this_world: The world is full of round motions: fans, wheels, and the Moon round the Earth. From the side, many of them look like back and forth.

roots.thread: We sorted motions into three kinds: straight, round, and back and forth. Then one bunch of keys showed two of the kinds at once. The kinds are names we give from where we watch, and one motion can fit more than one of them. Everything is conscious, and every watcher meets the world from their own place. A gecko on the wall, an ant on the floor and you each see the same fan move in a different path.

teachings.teaching: Kanada, an early Indian thinker, listed five kinds of motion: moving up, moving down, drawing in, spreading out, and going along.
teachings.link: Like us, Kanada sorted motions by the way they go. His list is different from ours. People can sort the same motions in more than one way.

teachings.source: Udana 6.4, a Buddhist text, and the Jain teaching of anekantavada, many-sidedness
teachings.teaching: Some blind people each touch a different part of an elephant. One says an elephant is like a rope, and another says like a wall. Each is right about the part they touched.
teachings.link: From above you saw a circle, and from the side a line. Each view told the truth about the keys from one place.

teachings.teaching: Aristotle, a Greek thinker, taught that everything that moves is moved by something.
teachings.link: In Who Starts It?, we asked the same question about each moving thing: what made it start?

science.text: A small swing's back-and-forth motion and a round motion seen from the side follow the same pattern. Scientists use circles to work out how swings and springs move.
Jupiter's four big moons go round Jupiter. From Earth we see their circles from the side, so they seem to go back and forth.

other_view.view: The keys had one real path, a circle. The back-and-forth line was only how it looked from one place, so it is not a second kind of motion.

practice.title: Back and forth with your breath
practice.say: Sit up tall. Put one hand on your tummy. Breathe in slowly and feel your tummy go out. Breathe out and feel it come back in. That is back and forth. Now draw a slow circle in the air in front of you, as big as a clock face. Do one round for each breath. A grown-up standing beside you sees your finger go only up and down.
practice.kid: Hand on your tummy. Breathe in. It goes out. Breathe out. It comes in. Now draw a slow circle in the air, one round for each breath.

ask: The keys went round, and they went back and forth. Which one was the real path, or were both real?

how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that things in the sky can go round something other than the Earth? This card tells what Galileo saw in 1610.
how_we_found_out.who: Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, and Simon Marius, a German astronomer
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Everything in the sky goes round the Earth. At first, Galileo also took Jupiter's moons for ordinary stars.
how_we_found_out.story: For a very long time, many people in Europe believed that everything in the sky went round the Earth. On 7 January 1610, Galileo Galilei, an Italian scientist, pointed his new telescope at the planet Jupiter. Beside it he saw three tiny bright points, in a straight line. At first he took them for stars. But the next night they had moved. Within a week he had seen four. Night after night, they moved back and forth along the same line, never going far from Jupiter. Sometimes one vanished behind Jupiter and later came out again. Galileo worked out what this meant. The four points were moons, going round and round Jupiter. We see their round paths from the side, so they seem to go back and forth. Here were things in the sky going round something that was not the Earth. Galileo wrote about them in a little book, The Starry Messenger, in March 1610. A German astronomer, Simon Marius, said he had seen the moons at about the same time. The names we use for them today, Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto, are the ones Marius printed.

founder: ideas/by_topic/forces-and-movement.md, 'Motion & Position': 'Skit of two observers debating who is moving' became the keys test and the Kavya and Farhan perspective question, 'swing a pendulum' became the shadow game, and 'journal of movements noticed today' became the Path Hunt.

The Level 1 unit on kinds of motion uses five ways of moving (roll, slide, spin, swing, bounce), a roll-or-slide push test, a bounce test, a swinging bag and a toy swing. This unit moves on to three paths and to what starts a motion, with a new main test (keys seen from two places), an eyes-shut walking test, a vibrating ruler, a seedling project and a circle-drawing challenge.
science: Uniform circular motion seen edge-on, or projected as a shadow, is simple harmonic motion, the same pattern as a small pendulum swing. Any introductory physics text.

Galileo Galilei, Sidereus Nuncius (The Starry Messenger), Venice, March 1610: observations of Jupiter's moons from 7 January 1610. Simon Marius, Mundus Iovialis, 1614, with the names Io, Europa, Ganymede and Callisto.
Souman, J. L., Frissen, I., Sreenivasa, M. N. and Ernst, M. O. (2009). Walking straight into circles. Current Biology 19, 1538-1542.
Phototropism in seedlings: auxin gathers on the shaded side and the shaded side grows faster. Any plant biology text.
Vaisheshika Sutra 1.1.7 on the five kinds of karma (motion). Udana 6.4 on the blind men and the elephant. Aristotle, Physics, Book 7, chapter 1.

playtest: I walked through each game with 2 players and with 4, each experiment, activity, project and challenge step by step as a family would in a flat, and every card and worksheet item on its own. I rewrote both card games so they end, work with a parent and one child, and ask for the answers they print. I made the shadow step and the eyes-shut line fit a flat, introduced every made-up name, cut repeated questions and checks, and tightened the jokes to 8.
